narrative: The model estimates a 66% chance that you will leave your job, meaning it considers departure more likely than not. That risk signal is why the promotion is denied: the organization is reluctant to invest in a role you may soon vacate. The most influential factor was your total years of experience. At 1–5 years, which is common among employees predicted to stay, this factor actually pushed the model toward “will stay,” not toward leaving. The second most important factor was that you have received other job opportunities while in this job. Only about 23% of employees predicted to stay had such opportunities, so this was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward leaving. Third, working in the “other” sector added a smaller push toward leaving; that sector is less common among employees predicted to stay, at about 22%. So although your experience level worked in your favor, the presence of outside opportunities and your sector outweighed it. Next, the organization should discuss your career path, retention and what would make you stay, while you should raise concerns about promotion criteria and future opportunities. The promotion decision should be reviewed alongside retention plans, not treated as a final judgment.
